lessons.title: Greetings and basic courtesies
lessons.objective: Greet people in Modern Standard Arabic and respond to common greetings.

tokens.grammarNote: Definite noun with the article اَلْ-. The final u-vowel ( ُ ) is the nominative case marker.
Preposition عَلَىَ ('upon') + the second-person plural pronoun كُمْ. A fixed religious and cultural greeting; the -kum ending makes it formal and addressed to a group.

question.prompt: When would you say ٱلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ ?
options: When you meet someone, as a general greeting.
Only when you are saying goodbye.
Only in writing, never in speech.
Only when you are asking someone for help.
question.correctExplanation: ٱلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ is the standard greeting used when meeting someone. The response is وَعَلَيْكُمُ ٱلسَّلَامُ ('and upon you, peace').
incorrectExplanations: Goodbye in Arabic is مَعَ ٱلسَّلَامَةِ (maʿa as-salāmati), not this greeting.
This is one of the most common spoken greetings in Arabic; it is not restricted to writing.
For asking help you would use phrases like سَاعِدْنِي (sāʿidnī, 'help me') or مِن فَضْلِكَ (min faḍlika, 'please').

tokens.grammarNote: Coordinating conjunction. Always written with a fatḥa on the wāw when connecting clauses: وَ.
Preposition عَلَىَ + second-person plural pronoun كُمْ + the nominative case marker ـُ.
Definite noun; the final -u marks nominative case in this construction.

question.prompt: What is the function of وَ at the start of this sentence?
options: It means 'and', linking this response to the previous greeting.
It is part of the word for 'you'.
It marks the sentence as a question.
It indicates that the speaker is female.
question.correctExplanation: وَ is the coordinating conjunction meaning 'and'. It links the response وَعَلَيْكُمُ ٱلسَّلَامُ back to the original greeting.
incorrectExplanations: The pronoun 'you (plural)' is embedded in عَلَيْكُمُ; the و is a separate conjunction.
Question marks in Arabic are usually indicated by intonation or a question particle like هَلْ, not by و.
Gender is not marked on و. Speaker gender is encoded in verbs and some pronouns elsewhere in speech.

tokens.grammarNote: Noun in the accusative case (tanwīn: ـًا). Means literally 'family' or 'people (of yours)' — a fixed welcoming expression.
Conjunction وَ + noun سَهْلًا ('ease', accusative). Together the phrase means 'welcome' — literally 'family and ease'.

question.prompt: How do you answer أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا when someone welcomes you?
options: أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا — you say the same phrase back.
You stay silent and nod.
You say شُكْرًا (thank you) only.
You say مَعَ ٱلسَّلَامَةِ (goodbye).
question.correctExplanation: The standard reply is to mirror the greeting: أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا. You can extend it to أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا بِكَ ('welcome to you').
incorrectExplanations: Silence is not a customary Arabic response to a welcome.
Thanking the host is polite, but the standard verbal reply is the same welcoming phrase.
مَعَ ٱلسَّلَامَةِ is a farewell, used when leaving.

lessons.title: Numbers one through four
lessons.objective: Recognize and pronounce the cardinal numbers 1–4 in Modern Standard Arabic.

tokens.grammarNote: Preposition عِنْدَ ('at, in the possession of') + the first-person singular possessive suffix ـِي ('my'). An idiomatic way to say 'I have'.
Noun in the nominative case, indefinite (tanwīn: ـٌ).
Cardinal number 'one', used for counting singular masculine nouns. Indefinite nominative (tanwīn: ـٌ).

options: One (1)
Two (2)
Three (3)
Ten (10)
question.correctExplanation: وَاحِدٌ (wāḥidun) means 'one'. Two is اِثْنَانِ, three is ثَلَاثَةٌ, ten is عَشَرَةٌ.
incorrectExplanations: Two in Arabic is اِثْنَانِ (ithnāni).
Three in Arabic is ثَلَاثَةٌ (thalāthatun).
Ten in Arabic is عَشَرَةٌ (ʿasharatun).

tokens.grammarNote: Adverbial preposition لَدَىَ + first-person singular possessive suffix ـَىَّ ('my'). A more formal way to say 'I have' than عِنْدِي.
Noun كِتَاب ('book') in the dual form: ـَانِ ending marks 'two'. The dual is exclusive to exactly two.

question.prompt: Why does كِتَابَانِ end in ـَانِ ?
options: It marks the dual — 'two books' specifically.
It marks the plural — 'many books'.
It is the feminine marker.
It marks the accusative case only.
question.correctExplanation: The suffix ـَانِ is the dual marker in Arabic, used for exactly two of something. كِتَاب + ـَانِ = 'two books'.
incorrectExplanations: Arabic plurals use ـُونَ / ـَاتٌ / اِفْتِعَال patterns, not ـَانِ.
The ـَانِ ending is for the dual; feminine is usually ـَةٌ or ـَاتٌ.
Dual nouns in Arabic take nominative case by default and have their own dedicated ending.

lessons.title: Basic directions
lessons.objective: Recognize basic directional words in Modern Standard Arabic.

sentences.english: The library is in front of the mosque.

tokens.grammarNote: Definite noun with the article اَلْ-. The final ـُ is the nominative case marker.
Preposition of place. Takes its object in the genitive case.
Definite noun in the genitive case ( ـِ ), governed by the preposition أَمَامَ.

options: in front of
behind
to the right of
next to
question.correctExplanation: أَمَامَ (amāma) means 'in front of'. Behind is وَرَاءَ, to the right is عَنْ يَمِينِ, and next to is بِجَانِبِ.
incorrectExplanations: Behind in Arabic is وَرَاءَ (warā'a).
To the right is عَنْ يَمِينِ (ʿan yamīni).
Next to / beside is بِجَانِبِ (bijānibi).

sentences.english: The school is behind the house.

tokens.grammarNote: Definite noun with the article اَلْ-. The final ـُ is the nominative case marker.
Preposition of place. Takes its object in the genitive case.
Definite noun in the genitive case ( ـِ ), governed by وَرَاءَ.

question.prompt: Why is ٱلْبَيْتِ written with a kasra (-i) at the end?
options: Because it follows the preposition وَرَاءَ and takes the genitive case.
Because it is the subject of the sentence.
Because it is a verb.
Because the article اَلْ- always takes a kasra.
question.correctExplanation: After prepositions like وَرَاءَ, the following noun takes the genitive case marker ـِ (kasra).
incorrectExplanations: The subject ٱلْمَدْرَسَةُ takes nominative ـُ, not ـِ.
ٱلْبَيْتِ is a noun, not a verb.
The article اَلْ- itself does not impose any case ending on the noun; the noun's case is determined by its grammatical role in the sentence.
